items.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: Hubert Laws, go out and do concerts with Jean Pierre Rampal

ctx.x: Right. They really are. Because like I said any subject matter you name, any one, anything, they’re doing it somewhere. Ophthalmology, they’re doing it. Optometry? Speak a different language? They’re doing it. Herbie Hancock, electrical engineer,

because I remember once he was talking because Oscar Peterson had a tremendous respect for Herbie. He said it in print. And he was talking about it one time. I got this video called “In the Key of Oscar.” This is a very good video. I don’t know if you can get it in the States, you might have to call the Institute of Canada in Toronto and get it. Mulgrew has it, and it’s Oscar doing a reunion with his family members because he had been estranged from a couple of his kids because he was so busy traveling and they…

items.title: Hubert Laws — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got the news during a rehearsal that I had with Harold Mabern

ctx.x: I Have a Dream. This was a time of – the ’60s – it’s the tail end of the ’60s. King has already been assassinated. We getting – it’s getting – things have got to change. We’re still striving to make things change. Herbie was capturing the Zeitgeist of the time. So I just wanted to bring that one up. But also ’69 is a significant date for you, because that’s when you had auditioned and were accepted into the – let’s talk about . . .

Metropolitan Opera Orchestra. Yes, that was the – I had auditioned, and I got the news during a rehearsal that I had with Harold Mabern, and I think it’s Bob Cranshaw’s son who was playing bass. I remember because my second bedroom was being used as a rehearsal studio. I got a call. We got two calls that day. One was about the fact that Wes Montgomery had passed. And the other one – so one was bad news, one was good news for me, because that was when I got accepted to play in that orchestra, the Met, which I…
